c.tagline: Djerba's whitewashed island capital of souks, seafront forts, and ancient synagogues.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps on Djerba; get around by metered yellow taxis (insist on the meter, or agree a price first) and shared louage minibuses that run set routes between the island's towns.

emergency.note: 197 reaches the national police/guard, 190 is the SAMU ambulance service, and 198 is Civil Protection (fire and rescue).

hood_landmark.Houmt Souk (Old Town): Borj El Ghazi Mustapha, Houmt Souk

avoid.reason: Expect persistent souk touts and tourist overcharging, with occasional pickpocketing in crowded market lanes.

hood_desc: The island's main town, a maze of whitewashed lanes, covered souks, old fondouk courtyards turned guesthouses, and the seafront Borj El Ghazi Mustapha fort; best for first-timers who want markets, history, and cafe life on foot.

A quiet inland village south of town famous for the ancient El Ghriba synagogue and the Djerbahood street-art murals painted across its houses; suits travelers drawn to heritage, art, and Djerba's layered Jewish and Berber culture.
Djerba's lively second town, known for its big weekly market, restaurants, and proximity to the resort strip; a good base for shopping, dining out, and beach access.
A calm stretch of the southeast coast lined with beach resorts, palm groves, and long sandy shore; ideal for a relaxed, all-inclusive-style seaside stay.
The island's main resort beach northeast of Houmt Souk, a long sweep of sand backed by thalasso spa hotels and water-sports; a quiet, sea-facing base close to town.

water.note: Drink bottled water; Djerba's tap water is brackish and not recommended.

transit.hours: Taxis and shared louages run through the day and early evening; service thins after dark, when taxis are the main option.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram, or rail on Djerba. Getting around means metered yellow taxis, shared louage minibuses between towns, and rental cars or scooters; the island connects to the mainland by the El Kantara causeway and the Ajim-Jorf ferry.
transit.pay: Taxi and louage fares are paid in cash (Tunisian dinars) to the driver; there is no transit card. Keep small notes handy.

bus: SNTRI intercity coaches to Tunis, Gabès and Medenine
Local buses and louage minibuses across the island
ferry: Ajim-Jorf car ferry to the Tunisian mainland (El Kantara causeway also links the island by road)
train: No rail on the island; nearest railhead is Gabès on the mainland

transit.m: Rental car pickup at the terminal

tip.r: Around 10% at restaurants is customary; small tips for guides, drivers, hotel staff and hammam attendants are expected.

landmarks: Borj El Ghazi Mustapha (Borj El Kebir fortress)
A 13th-century seafront fortress rebuilt by Ottoman corsairs, its honey-colored ramparts overlook the fishing harbour and recall Djerba's turbulent pirate-era history.
Houmt Souk Central Market (the souks)
A maze of whitewashed lanes and vaulted stalls where fish auctions, spice sellers and carpet merchants keep Djerba's centuries-old trading traditions vividly alive.
El Ghriba Synagogue (Erriadh)
Africa's most famous synagogue, a serene blue-tiled sanctuary that draws Jewish pilgrims each Lag BaOmer and claims foundations dating back over two millennia.
Djerbahood (Erriadh street-art village)
An open-air gallery where international artists have splashed murals across the whitewashed alleys of Erriadh, turning a sleepy village into a photographer's dream.
Fondouks of Houmt Souk (historic caravanserais)
Galleried courtyard inns once sheltering traveling merchants and their camels, now atmospheric hotels and cafés that preserve the town's caravan-trade soul.
Mosque of the Turks (Jamaa Ettrouk)
An Ottoman-era mosque whose dazzling white domes and distinctive pointed minaret make it Houmt Souk's most photogenic religious silhouette.
Guellala Museum (Djerba Heritage Museum)
A hilltop museum showcasing Djerban weddings, costumes and crafts, with sweeping views over the island's olive groves and pottery workshops below.
Djerba Explore Park and Lalla Hadria Museum
A cultural park pairing one of Africa's largest Nile crocodile farms with a superb museum of Islamic and Tunisian art spanning thirteen centuries.
Sidi Mahrez Beach (Plage Sidi Mahres)
Djerba's signature stretch of powdery white sand and shallow turquoise water, fringed by palms along the island's resort-lined northeastern coast.
Flamingo Island (Ras R'mel peninsula)
A sandy spit reached by pirate-style boat trips from the harbour, where pink flamingos gather in winter on dazzling shallow lagoons.

train.note: Djerba has no railway of its own - SNCFT's southern main line ends at Gabès, about 70 km northwest of the island (https://www.sncft.com.tn/). From Gabès you continue by louage or bus to El Jorf and cross to the island by ferry, so rail is only useful as the Tunis-Gabès leg of a longer trip. The direct Tunis-Houmt Souk coach is through-ticketed and simpler than combining train and road. There are no international trains from anywhere in southern Tunisia.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the bus station in the centre of Houmt Souk, a few minutes' walk from the souk and the harbour. SNTRI runs the Tunis-Houmt Souk service in roughly 8 hours including overnight departures, and the fare includes the Jorf-Ajim ferry crossing; tickets are bought at the station counter rather than online. Shared louages from the adjacent stand cover Gabès, Medenine, Zarzis and Tataouine and leave when full. No scheduled international coach serves the island - the Libyan border at Ras Ajdir is reached by louage via Ben Gardane, and Algeria means going back through Tunis.

intl.to: Jorf, mainland Tunisia (Tunisia) - sails from Ajim, about 22 km southwest of Houmt Souk
intl.op: state-run bac (car ferry) — tickets sold at the ramp, no online booking

ferry.note: The Ajim-Jorf bac crosses the narrow strait in about 20 minutes, running roughly every 15-30 minutes by day and much less often overnight; foot passengers pay almost nothing and cars a small toll. Nothing is bookable in advance - you simply queue - and vehicle queues get long on summer weekends and around Eid. The alternative is the Roman causeway from El Kantara at the island's southeast corner, which needs no boat but adds distance if you are coming from Gabès. There are no international sailings from Djerba; Tunisia's ferries to Europe leave from La Goulette in Tunis with CTN (https://www.ctn.com.tn/).

half.name: Midoun
half.blurb: Djerba's largest market town, about 16 kilometers away, known for its bustling Friday souk selling spices, textiles, and local crafts.

half.name: Zarzis
half.blurb: A coastal town south of Djerba with palm and olive groves, sandy beaches, and a smaller, quieter souk than Houmt Souk's.

full.name: Matmata
full.blurb: A mainland Berber town of underground troglodyte dwellings carved into the rock, roughly two and a half hours from Djerba.

full.name: Ksar Ghilane
full.blurb: A Sahara oasis with natural hot springs and dunes reached by a desert crossing from the mainland, popular for camel rides and 4x4 trips.
